scene: 4.1 Garage: The Signal Is Not Noise

lines.text: Around seven megahertz... this band should not be this clean tonight.
Wait. There are intervals inside the noise. It is not random.
Three short pulses, two long ones, then a pause. It is repeating.
A normal amateur station would not hide a pulse pattern under static.
This is not ordinary noise.
It sounds like Morse code, but something else follows it. Numbers. Symbols.
Who would send something like this at 2:17 a.m. on this band?
Record everything first. Frequency, spacing, waveform. Do not miss anything.
The last part changed. The front is mixed code, but this final part is pure Morse.
U-n-l-e-s-s... unless.
Decoded. Plan. Fails.
Unless decoded, the plan fails.
Unless it is decoded, the plan fails.
This does not sound like a chat message. It sounds like an instruction left for whoever receives it.
If the sender expected someone to hear it, there must be a next step.
The sentence was simple, but it pulled the whole room toward Antarctica.

scene: 4.3 Video Call: The Antarctic Star Plan

lines.text: Jiang Che? Do you know what time it is?
Two forty. Dad, I received a signal.
Seven-megahertz band, mixed code. The last line is an English conditional sentence.
Unless decoded, the plan fails.
Did you decode the earlier pulses?
Not yet. I only read the last line. The front format is unfamiliar, almost like a custom protocol.
Jiang Che, that is the test signal we buried ten years ago.
What test?
The Antarctic Star Plan. Ten years ago, we placed a signal transmitter beneath the Antarctic ice.
It sends test signals on a schedule, using a mixed code we designed.
Why would you do that?
To see whether someone could decode it independently, without being told what it was.
If no one could decode it, the plan would remain dormant.
If someone could, it would mean the next generation might be ready to protect Antarctica.
So you have been waiting?
Waiting for anyone young enough to inherit the question. This time, you heard it.
So the Antarctic map on my wall was not just a map?
You knew this day might come?
We did not know who would receive it, or whether anyone ever would.
But we hoped the receiver would be more than clever. We hoped they would be responsible.
I thought Antarctica was just your work. It has been waiting for a receiver all along.
It has been waiting for someone who can hear the whole signal and think about the consequences.
What do I need to do?
Record everything first. Do not explain it too soon, and do not make it public.
Continue decoding. The earlier layers should contain coordinates and the next instruction.
But understand this. Once you start, there may be no easy way back.
I am scared, but I do not want to stop.
If this is the signal you left behind, I will decode it completely.
Jiang Che.
How did you get in?
The door was not locked. The teacher asked me to bring your mock exam paper.
You have missed class for three straight days. Your homeroom teacher said you were sick.
But this does not look like rest.
Put the paper there. I will look at it later.
What is that?
An amateur radio project.
An amateur radio project does not usually say the plan fails.
You misunderstood it. It is only an encoded sentence.
I did not misunderstand it. The student council just finished safety training. An English instruction like that cannot be treated as a joke.
It is not a threat.
Then explain it clearly. Radio signals, encrypted communication, and unknown sources all need to be reported to a faculty adviser.
This is personal.
Your personal matter has already cost you six classes.
If you do not come to the science club now, I will report it as a possible safety incident.
You would really do that?
I would. If you are actually in danger, I cannot pretend I did not see it.
Fine. I will go.
A mixed coded signal on the seven-megahertz band? Are you sure it was not ordinary shortwave interference?
Ordinary interference would not keep a stable pulse for four minutes, and it would not switch to English Morse at the end.
Can you show us the decoding process?
Yes. The raw signal has three layers.
The first layer is Morse code. It gave me the final English sentence.
The second layer is a number key. It turns time, frequency, and pulse intervals into a sequence.
Wait. You said it is not a threat. What is your evidence?
A threat usually demands immediate action. This sentence is conditional.
The key word is unless. It is not a countdown. It is a condition.
Unless decoded, the plan fails. The plan only continues if someone decodes it.
So the sentence is both an English grammar sample and an operation clue.
Exactly. Unless plus a reduced passive clause, then the main clause. The sender made the last line easy to read on purpose.
That explains the English sentence, but it does not prove the earlier layers are safe.
Good question. Jiang Che, what about the third layer?
The third layer is the strangest. It is not a standard code. It is a custom symbol layer.
I tried ASCII, Base64, and Caesar shifts. None of them worked.
Then I overlaid the symbol outlines on an Antarctic terrain map. They matched.
This one resembles the Antarctic Peninsula. This one resembles the Ross Ice Shelf.
So the sender hid geographic information inside the symbols.
Yes. It is not a threat. It is a coordinate clue.
If it is a coordinate clue, why not send a map directly?
Because it is not for everyone. It is only for someone who can decode it step by step.
From the frequency, code structure, and geographic mapping, it looks more like a scientific test signal.
So plan does not mean an attack plan?
More likely a protection plan. A plan waiting to continue after it is decoded.
I need more evidence.
But I will not report it to the administration for now.
Jiang Che, if this involves school resources, off-campus action, or any safety risk, you tell me first.
Including my safety?
Including everyone's safety.
The Antarctic Peninsula... southwest of Great Wall Station.
Sixty-two degrees, twelve minutes, fifty-nine seconds south. Fifty-eight degrees, fifty-seven minutes, fifty-two seconds west.
It is a coordinate.
The point was about two hundred kilometers from Great Wall Station, near the area where his parents had last worked ten years ago.
What did they leave there?
Tomorrow at three p.m., science club meeting room. Bring all your materials.
I thought you needed more evidence.
I have seen enough risk.
So you are going to report it?
No. I will join.
Do not investigate this alone.
Are you sure? This may be bigger than a school project.
I know. That is why you cannot keep doing it alone.
You do not need no one. You are just used to no one helping you.
I work faster alone.
Staying up all night, skipping class, and putting a dangerous signal on your wall is not efficiency.
I do not understand radio the way you do, but I understand procedure, evidence, and risk control.
If this is real, we need to record the source, organize the files, and decide who can know and who cannot.
If it is fake, we still need evidence proving it is fake.
Are you planning to manage me?
I am planning to stop you from turning this into something no one can control.
I handle procedure, files, and safety. You handle decoding.
Then what are we?
For now, a project team.
Okay.
In the dark, the signal continued.
